Their opponents objected that this matching happens only in imagination, and only if both series can be pictured there. But an endless series cannot be pictured in imagination. Nor do the events exist all together in reality, so they cannot be matched there either. The proof, then, depends on something that exists neither in imagination nor in reality. They also objected that the increase and decrease are assumed at the finite end of the series, not at the endless end whose size is in dispute. So this does not prove what it is meant to prove. That is the argument and the objections given here.

I say that every event can be described in two ways: it comes before what follows it, and after what came before it. These are different ways of considering the event. If we look at past events starting from now, treating each event once as earlier than what follows it and once as later than what came before it, the two series—earlier events and later events—match exactly in reality, though we consider them in different ways. We do not need to imagine matching them term by term.

Even so, the earlier events must be more numerous than the later ones on the side now in dispute: the past. So the later events must be finite, ending before the earlier events do. The earlier events exceed them by a finite number, so they too must be finite. That concludes his argument.

One more issue remains. In any number, such as ten, there must be an order—not between its first, second, and third members, but among one, two, and three themselves. One comes before two by nature, even though it does not come before itself. Likewise, two comes before three, and three before four. So if an infinite number existed, as some have believed about rational souls, then its members would be together and ordered, and the matching argument would apply. Unless, of course, we deny that any number other than one comes before another number. Avicenna discusses this in the Metaphysics of The Healing.

The third argument is this. If causes and effects stretched back forever, without ending in a first cause that causes but is not itself caused, then there would be a whole made up of all existing possible things, each caused by another member of that whole. That whole would itself be an existing possible thing.

It exists because its members exist, and a whole does not cease to exist unless one of its parts ceases to exist. It is possible because it depends on a possible member. Anything that depends on something possible is itself possible. By defining the whole as all existing possible things, we exclude what does not exist and what exists necessarily.
You might object that a group made up of existing parts can be only an idea, with no existence in reality—for example, a person and a stone taken together, or the sky and the earth.

To this we reply: They do not mean that the whole exists as one thing whose existence is separate from the existence of its parts. In fact, they have explicitly said that a whole existing in the outside world may have no nature distinct from that of its individual members, as with ten men taken together. A whole may also have a form that makes it a particular kind of thing, as in compounds made from the elements. Or it may have no such form and add only an arrangement of its parts, as with a bed made of pieces of wood. We will return to that example.

If the whole is itself an existing possible thing, then its independent cause—the cause that brings it into existence without relying on anything else—is either the whole itself, which is clearly impossible; one of its parts, which is also impossible; or something outside it. If the whole caused itself, one of its parts would have to cause itself and the causes on which it depends. Causing the whole means causing the parts that make it up, and an independent cause is one that needs nothing else. If something outside the whole causes it, that cause must bring at least some of its parts into existence. The chain of effects would then end at that cause, since anything outside the chain of possible things must exist necessarily in itself.

That part cannot also be caused by another part of the whole. Two independent causes cannot produce the same effect, and here we are speaking of a cause that brings its effect into existence on its own. This would contradict our assumptions in two ways: we assumed that the chain has no first cause, and that every member is caused by another member.

This account also answers the objections to the proof. First, if by “the cause of the whole chain” we mean its complete cause—the set of conditions that fully account for it—then it need not be impossible for the chain itself to be that cause. It would be impossible only if the cause had to come before the whole. But the complete cause of a composite does not have to come before it; indeed, it cannot, since the parts that make up the effect are included in that complete cause. One might object that this would make the cause necessary in itself, since it would exist through itself. That does not follow. It would follow only if the cause did not depend on a part distinct from itself, whether or not we call that part “something else.”

If instead we mean the efficient cause—the agent that brings the whole into existence—then it could be one of the parts of the chain. That would be impossible only if it had to cause every part, including itself and the causes on which it depends. But it need not: a part of a composite effect may come from something other than its efficient cause, as the wood in a bed comes from a different source than the carpenter. Even if we grant that point, we still cannot assume that whatever lies outside the chain must exist necessarily. There could be infinitely many chains of causes and effects, each depending on a cause outside itself that belongs to another chain, with no chain reaching the Necessary Being. Or, even if every chain must ultimately depend on the Necessary Being, that does not rule out an infinite series: the totality of infinitely many causes and effects could itself be a possible thing that depends on the Necessary Being.

There is also a more general objection. The whole could be made up of the Necessary Being and all existing possible things. Its cause would be neither itself, nor one of its parts, nor something outside it. If the Necessary Being were outside this whole, it might seem to become caused if there were more than one Necessary Being. And if the cause were one of the parts, either it would cause every part, bringing two independent causes to the same effect, or it would cause only some of them.

Our answer is that we have clearly defined the whole as all existing possible things, with each part caused by another part. The only thing outside it is the Necessary Being. The least that follows from its being an independent cause is that at least one part of the whole is caused by something outside it alone, not by another part. That is what it means for the chain to end. The independent cause cannot itself be one of the parts, because then it would have to cause itself and its own causes. If something else caused some of its parts, then neither cause would be independent: each would depend on the other for the whole to exist. This differs from a whole made up of the Necessary Being and possible things, since one part—the Necessary Being—exists through itself and depends on nothing else. And a bed’s independent maker is not the carpenter alone, but the carpenter together with whoever produced the wood.

There is, however, an objection to the claim that the independent cause of a composite made up of possible parts must cause every part. If this means that the very same cause acts independently on each part, it cannot be right. The parts of a composite may come into being one by one, as when the pieces of wood and then the arrangement that makes a bed are formed. If the independent cause were absent when the first part appeared, the effect would come before its cause. If the cause were already present, the final part of the effect would come after its independent cause, even though the cause was supposed to produce it immediately. We have already seen why that is impossible.

Alternatively, “cause every part” might mean that the cause of the whole produces each part either directly or through one of its own parts, so no part depends on anything outside it. If the effect is composite, then its independent cause would also have parts, each arising at the same time as its corresponding part of the effect. There would be no cause that comes before its effect and no effect delayed after its cause. But this does not prove what is needed: it does not show that the independent cause of the chain cannot be one of its parts. A part of the chain could be a cause in this sense without causing itself or its own causes. That part would be the whole made up of all the members that are both causes and effects, leaving out only the final effect—the one that comes after the rest in the order of causation, but before them in rank when we count from the finite end. This whole is sometimes described as what comes before the final effect, and sometimes as what comes after the first effect. It is a part of the chain. When it exists, the chain exists, and each part of that whole corresponds to a part of the chain. So its causing the chain does not mean that anything causes itself.

One might object that this whole, which serves as the cause, is itself possible and therefore needs a cause. The answer is that its cause is the whole before the final effect within it; and likewise, each earlier whole is caused by the whole before it, without end.

One might also object that the part of the chain preceding its final effect cannot be an independent cause, since it is itself possible and needs a cause. The same would apply to every whole we propose. The chain would therefore exist only with help from those other causes. And that whole would not be enough to make the chain exist, since the pure effect would also have to be included.

We reply that this does not undermine independence. Independence means that a cause does not need help from a cause outside it in order to bring something about. We have supposed that the cause of each whole lies within it. And clearly, its final effect plays no part in bringing that whole into existence.

Someone might say: If by “the whole” you mean either one chain or infinitely many chains, as you proposed, then this objection goes away too: there is no final effect and no composite whole before it. We reply that the objection still applies. The cause of this whole is the part made up of all the infinitely many wholes that come before their infinitely many final effects. If you say that, from the start, we denied that the cause of the whole could be one of its parts—because no part has a better claim than another, or because any part you choose has a stronger claim to be the cause since it has greater causal power—we reply that this is not so. The part made up of everything before the final effect is the one fit to be the cause, since none of the other parts can independently bring the whole into existence.

This way of arguing against an endless chain and proving the Necessary Being is very weak. We have already shown that the existence of each thing is the same as its unity, and that a thing’s unity is the same as its existence, in the sense explained earlier. So it is wrong to say that a person and a stone together exist as a third thing, separate from both. This also raises another objection to the original proof: we do not accept that the proposed whole needs a cause beyond the causes of its individual parts. That would follow only if the whole had an existence different from the existence of its parts, each of which has its own cause. Calling the whole “possible” does not prove anything. It is the possible things that exist, each through its own cause. Why, then, would the whole need another cause? Ten separate units, for example, do not need a cause beyond the causes of the units themselves.

To say that the existence of all the parts differs from the existence of each part is empty talk. The fact that all the parts together are different from any one part does not mean that the whole has an existence outside the mind beyond the existence of its parts. It is true that a real composite ceases to exist if one of its parts ceases to exist: each real composite has its own nature and its own unity, and losing a part destroys it. But this does not mean that any combination the mind imagines between two things becomes real as soon as both things exist, and then disappears only if one of them disappears. Also, the fact that something does not exist when one of its conditions is absent does not always mean that it exists whenever that condition is present.

This shows why a later claim—that a thing can cause itself—is false. The claim says that all existing things, both possible and necessary, form one possible whole because it depends on its members, and that this whole has no cause except itself. Its cause would have to be one of its parts, which is impossible because it depends on the remaining parts; or something outside it. But nothing lies outside it, so they conclude that it causes itself. There is no problem here, they say, because the whole’s dependence on each individual part does not mean that it depends on itself as a whole. However, if by “cause” they mean an independent agent that brings things into existence, then that cause is one part of the whole of all existing things: either the Necessary Being, or what lies before the final effect and ultimately reaches the Necessary Being.

They also say that it is impossible for a thing to cause itself, or to do something equivalent to that, when the cause must come before its effect. In that case, the thing would have to come before itself. But it is not always impossible for a thing to be the complete cause of itself. As explained earlier, this happens in the whole made up of the Necessary Being and its first effect, or of the Necessary Being and all its effects.

That argument is plainly weak. A sound mind cannot make sense of something that is possible in itself and yet does not need anything beyond itself in order to exist. If the whole they call possible had an existence different from the existence of its individual members, and a possibility different from theirs, then it would need a cause different from the causes of its members. To say that its existence is different while its cause is the same adds nothing.

One careful thinker says: We can take several things together as one whole, and use a singular word for them, such as “the group” or “the whole.” Or we can consider them one by one, using words such as “this one” and “that one.” The two ways of looking at them can lead to different judgments. For example, a narrow house cannot hold a group of people all at once, though it can hold them one after another. Knowing this, we can choose to explain what makes the two individuals exist together by looking at them separately: the whole depends on each of its two parts, and together the parts are enough for it to exist. So this one and that one are the two causes that make their whole exist. If we then consider the two separately, each is possible and needs a cause.

I say that this careful thinker got part of the matter right and part wrong. He was right that, taken separately, the two are neither one possible thing nor one necessary thing. They are two things: one is necessary, and the other is possible and exists through it. He was wrong to think that taking things together or separately changes what exists outside the mind. Whether the mind considers the sky and the earth together or one by one, their reality outside the mind does not change. Only our way of thinking about them changes. The mind can consider them as one thing that exists in thought, but that does not make them one thing in the outside world. The imagination can divide the sky into two, but that makes it two only in thought, not in reality. Taking things together or separately changes how we view them, not the things themselves.

The house example does not show a difference between looking at things as a whole and looking at them separately. The difference is in what we say about the group. The group, whether considered together or one by one, can be said to fit in the house if its members enter at different times. It cannot be said to fit if they all enter at once. That is the point here.

Some also object that this leads to an endless series of things as soon as we suppose that two things exist. The objection does not apply. Considering two things as a whole does not mean considering them again together with the feature of “being together”; that would count the parts of their nature twice. By “the whole” we mean the two things that bear the shared arrangement, without adding “being arranged together” as another part. So someone who says that the two things exist as something distinct from each of them need not say that their togetherness, or their being two, exists as yet another thing. One thing can exist even if “oneness”—the feature of being one—does not exist as a separate thing.

Someone might ask: Many philosophers say that number exists and is not the same as all its individual units taken together. How, then, can you say that a composite has no existence beyond the existence of its units? We reply: number exists in the sense that many units exist in reality. We do not agree that number is something different from all the units taken together; it is those very units. But treating number and being many as if they were one thing with properties of their own—being ten, being a square, being odd, being a perfect number, and so on—is an act of the mind. These properties do have something in reality that they refer to: the existence of many units.

The fourth argument rests on two terms that go together: cause and effect. If the chain of causes and effects did not end in a cause that was not itself caused, then cause and effect would not match. But that is impossible, so the starting assumption must be false. Put another way: if cause and effect match, the chain must end in a cause that is not itself caused. Cause and effect do match, so the chain must end.

They match because, whenever one exists—in the mind or in reality—the other exists too, and when one is absent, so is the other. Why does this mean the chain must end? The final effect is only an effect; everything before it is both an effect and a cause. If the chain never reached a cause that was not itself an effect, there would be an effect that was not also a cause.

Someone might object that the cause paired with a pure effect—the final effect, which causes nothing further—is simply the cause immediately above it, not a cause that is itself uncaused. We agree. But the point is that every effect must have a cause to match it. That requires there to be a cause that is not itself an effect. Some express this argument in two ways. First, if the chain went on forever, it would contain more effects than causes, which is impossible if cause and effect must match. Every cause in the chain is itself an effect, by assumption; but not every effect is also a cause. The final effect is the exception. Second, take all the causes in the chain and all its effects, and compare the two groups. If one group has more members than the other, cause and effect do not match. If they have the same number, then there must be a cause with no effect to match it, since at the finite end there is an effect that is not also a cause. Either way, the claim that the chain has no uncaused cause leads to a contradiction.

The fifth argument is close to the previous one. Remove the final effect from the proposed chain. Then count each remaining thing twice: once as a cause and once as an effect, since the same thing plays a different role when it causes something and when something causes it. This gives us two groups, considered in different ways: the causes and the effects. When we compare them, the cause group must have one more level. A cause always comes before its effect, so each cause matches the effect of the cause one level before it, not the effect at its own level. The final effect was left out, and it is not itself a cause. So the causes have one more level than the effects. If they did not, a cause would not come before its effect, as it must. A level of cause with no matching effect would mean that the chain ends.

The sixth argument uses the gaps between ordered things. It can be applied to causes and effects and to other things arranged in order. The interval between the final effect, or something like it, and each item in the chain must be finite, since it is bounded at both ends. The argument then says the whole chain must be finite: it can be only one item longer than a finite interval. For example, if the distance from the start of a road to every point along it is no more than a mile, the whole road cannot be more than a mile long, apart from a final segment at its end. If the starting point is not counted as part of the distance, there may be two extra segments.

This may persuade someone who accepts the intuitive step, but it does not force an opponent to agree. The opponent may reject the idea that a bounded interval in an ordered chain must contain only a finite number of steps. In a road, the distance from the start to any point is finite. But if the chain has infinitely many steps, the opponent can say that there is no last point before another point that would make the interval finite.

The argument tries to prove this by saying that a total made from finite numbers must itself be finite. That is weak: it simply repeats the claim, and in a less clear form. A total made directly from individual units is more obviously finite than a total made from groups, each of which contains a finite number of units. But the opponent can still object that this works only if there are finitely many groups, which has not been shown. This can mislead us into thinking that because each part is finite, the whole must be finite. That does not follow.

The seventh proof is this. Any infinite series, whether it is a chain of causes and effects or something else, must contain groups of a thousand. The number of thousand-groups in it must either equal or exceed the number of individual units. Both are clearly impossible, because there must be a thousand units for each thousand-group. For example, one hundred thousand units make one hundred groups of a thousand.

The other possibility is that there are fewer thousand-groups than individual units. Then the individual units divide into two groups: one as large as the number of thousand-groups, and the rest. The first group must lie either toward the finite end of the series or toward its infinite end. Either way, the whole series would have to be finite. If the series is infinite in both directions, mark a point in it. This gives us a finite end, and we can use the same two possibilities.

In the first case, the number of thousand-groups is finite because it lies between two limits: the finite end of the series and the point where the second group begins. If the number of thousand-groups is finite, the whole series is finite, since it is made up of a finite number of groups, each containing a finite number of units. In the second case, the group made up of the excess units lies toward the finite end. It contains 999 times as many units as there are thousand-groups, and is bounded by the end of the series and the start of the thousand-groups. So this group too is finite. The number of thousand-groups must then be finite, and with it the whole series.

An objection to this proof, and to some of the earlier and later ones, is that the claim “equal, greater, or less” may not apply: equality and difference are features of finite numbers. If equality means only that each part of one group has a matching part in the other, we do not agree that this is impossible for infinite groups. For example, the numbers from one onward can match the numbers from ten onward, even though the second group starts later and the first has nine more numbers. Even if we accept that objection, we can deny that the smaller group has a definite end. If the series is infinite, the part toward the infinite end is infinite too, as are its groups of thousands, hundreds, or tens. The claim that there are two groups, with one ending where the other begins, is false.

The eighth proof rests on the order of the series. In any ordered chain of causes and effects, if one member is removed, every member after it must also disappear. So an actual chain made up entirely of effects must contain a cause that comes first among the causes. Without it, all the later levels that depend on it would disappear too. If we suppose there is an upward chain with no first cause, the whole chain would disappear. That contradicts our assumption that every member in the chain is an effect. In short, it makes no sense to say both that every member in the chain is caused by what comes before it and that no single cause supports the whole chain.

The ninth proof is the shortest, and the strongest, according to al-Fārābī. Every member of an actually existing ordered chain that goes on without end is such that it exists only if another member before it already exists. So all the infinite members of the chain would have to wait for something before them to exist. Reason asks: Where, then, can anything in the chain begin to exist, so that another thing can follow it?

The tenth proof is this. The proposed infinite chain of causes and effects must be either even or odd. If it is even, the next number is odd and has one more member; if it is odd, the next number is even and has one more. Any number that is less than another must be finite, since it is bounded by two ends: its beginning and the next member beyond it.

One might object that not every number that cannot be divided into two equal groups is odd. That is true only of finite numbers, since even and odd apply only to finite numbers. Another way to put the proof is to say that any number can be increased, so it is always less than another number. The flaw in that claim is clear.

The proofs above show that an ordered chain cannot extend without end in the direction of causes and causal priority. They do not show that it cannot extend without end in the direction of effects. The reason is that, if an ascending chain of causes had no first member, reason could not identify any cause that must exist first and from which the whole ordered chain could begin to exist. This is what makes such a chain impossible. A descending chain of effects is different.

The same point applies to all the proofs given earlier, including those based on one-to-one comparison, reciprocal relations, and the different ways things can be causes or effects. In each case, the chain is judged impossible only when two conditions come together: its members are ordered, and they all exist together in actuality at the infinite end of the chain. As noted earlier, the difference is that ordered causes exist in the world alongside the thing they cause, while their priority over it is established by analysis and by the mind's way of considering them.

If the ascending chain had no end, all its infinitely many causes would be supposed to exist at the same level as the effect and together with it. So both order and co-existence would be present at the level of the effect. In a descending chain, however, the ordered effects do not all exist together at the level of their cause. An effect's own incomplete, dependent existence does not become actual at the level of the cause's complete, causal existence. The cause is different: its existence is necessary at the level of the effect and encompasses it.

So order and co-existence at a prior level occur only in a chain that rises toward its causes, not in one that descends toward its effects. The proofs establish that the chain must end in the first direction, but not in the second. This is the gist of what our teacher, Sayyid, explained.
V. Why the Chain of Causes Must Have an End

The proofs given so far show that causes are finite in every respect, that each chain has a first principle, and that there is one first principle for all of them. The efficient and final causes come before the material and formal causes. In cases where the agent and its goal are not the same, the goal comes before the other causes, because it is what makes the agent act. Once we have shown that the chains of efficient and final causes are finite, the chains of material and formal causes must be finite too, since they come before the other two in this respect. The form, in one sense, is also an efficient cause, so it belongs with the final cause in that class. The proof that the chain of agents is finite can therefore also show that every level of causes is finite.

Since this proof has usually been applied to efficient causes, let us prove that the causes that are parts of a thing's existence and come before it in time are finite too. These are specifically called elements, because an element is a part that remains in a thing while it is still only potential.

First, if one thing is present in another in its entirety, we do not say that the second thing came from the first. A human being, for example, is present in full in a person who writes; we do not say that the writer came from humanity. When one thing depends on another in every respect, we do not say that it came from what it depends on. Nor do we say that white came from black, since no part of blackness remains in whiteness. So when something comes after something else in every respect, we do not say it came from that earlier thing.

But when some parts of one thing remain in another and other parts do not, we can say that the second came from the first. We say that air came from water, for example, because water is not present in air in its entirety, though part of it remains. We also say that white came from black, or that a chair came from wood, because the wood must change before it becomes a chair. So for one thing to be said to come from another, two things must be true: it must depend on some part of the earlier thing, and it must not remain together with another part of it.

With this use of the word in mind, matter can mean either the part that receives a form or what can become such a part—for example, water that can become air. In that change, what received the form of water becomes able to receive the form of air.

The first kind of matter must be finite. If every receiver had another receiver before it without end, one essence would have infinitely many parts. That is impossible. The second kind of matter can be explained as follows. The matter of air can receive the form of water, and the matter of water can receive the form of air. Each kind can change into the other. Neither kind, simply as a kind, must come before the other; a particular portion of water may come before a particular portion of air. We do not rule out an endless sequence of materials in this second sense. Each particular thing may come from another particular thing before it, as the points in a continuous motion follow one another without existing all together. There is no contradiction in that sequence having no end.

Formal causes, however, must be finite for two reasons. First, the final form is a cause of the form before it, so if forms had no end, neither would causes. Second, forms are parts of an essence, and one essence cannot have infinitely many parts.

Matter—the subject in which a thing's existence is possible—has two kinds. When a quality appears in a subject, it either causes something already present there to disappear or it does not. If it does not, the new quality is not a substantial form, the kind of form that makes the subject what it is. If it were such a form, the subject would have needed another substantial form before it appeared. That earlier form would either remain or disappear. If it remained, the subject would already be constituted by it and would not need the new form; the new quality would be an accident, not a substantial form. If the earlier form disappeared, the new form would have caused something to disappear, contrary to our starting assumption.

So any quality that appears in a subject without removing something already there is an accident, not a substantial form. We know that a thing's qualities, unless imposed on it or acquired by chance, arise by nature. There must therefore be a substantial form in the subject that leads it toward that accident. The substantial form is the first stage of its perfection, and the accident is the next.

By their nature, forms move toward their full perfection through accidents, unless something blocks them or a needed condition is absent. An accident that replaces another may be a block; seeds that do not sprout without sunlight are an example of a missing condition. Once a thing reaches its perfection, its nature cannot turn it back toward deficiency, because one and the same nature cannot both draw it toward something and turn it away. This proves that whenever a quality appears in a subject without displacing anything already there, the subject naturally moves toward it and cannot move away once it has attained it. A boy, for example, naturally grows into adulthood; once he has become a man, he cannot return to the seminal stage.

In The Healing, Avicenna raises an objection here. Someone who has no belief about a question may come to believe something false about it. Since that belief does not perfect the mind, does this not refute the claim that every quality that appears in a subject without making something disappear is a perfection?

I reply that a false belief can, in one respect, complete some simple-minded souls, because it is a positive state, and existence is better than nonexistence. It is harmful because it destroys the mind's readiness for the perfection proper to reason. In this respect it is like a poisonous quality: it completes an element but harms an animal. The same is true of blameworthy traits such as injustice and greed. They may complete some lower powers of the soul, but they diminish the higher power of reason.

False belief is a mental image and a positive state, so it can complete the intellect while it is still bound up with imagination. What offers no perfection at all is simple ignorance: it is not a quality but the absence of one.

In the other kind of change, a quality appears in a subject and causes something to disappear. What disappears may be a substantial form, as when air replaces water; a quality, as when black replaces white; or a quantity or shape. These cases are clear. In general, anyone who allows reversal in this second kind does so because matter can change from water into air and then back again. The first kind is different, because a thing's essence cannot change into another essence.

It follows, the argument says, that changes in the first kind cannot be reversed, while changes in the second kind can be. Someone might object that this division is incomplete. The transformation of elements into plants and animals cannot belong to the first kind, since such changes can be reversed: plants and animals can become elements again. But it cannot belong to the second kind either, because in that kind a new quality must remove an existing, opposite quality. The coming of a plant or animal into being does not seem to remove any such contrary quality.

The answer is that a single element is not ready to receive an animal form, for example. It becomes ready only when a balanced mixture arises, and that mixture replaces the element's pure, strong qualities. The mixture's relation to those pure qualities is therefore an instance of the second kind of change, which can be reversed. Once the mixture exists, however, receiving an animal form perfects it. This is like a boy growing into a man: he naturally moves toward adulthood and never moves back from it. Animal life does not begin until the body has first become a suitable mixture, just as a man does not become a boy and an embryo again. The development of an animal therefore involves both kinds of change and is not outside the two kinds of matter.

There is another way to divide matter. A subject may receive a form on its own, as basic matter receives bodily form, or it may receive a form together with something else. In the second case, those things must come together in some kind of composition. The composition may involve a change, or it may not. When it does, one change may be enough to reach the result, or several changes may be needed. When no change is involved, examples include a syllogism formed by joining premises, or a number formed by joining units. The units may be limited in number, as in these examples, or unlimited, as with an army.

On careful reflection, we can see that when a quality appears in matter without replacing anything, that matter has no settled nature of its own. Anything with a settled nature becomes matter for something else only after its nature disappears. This shows that the elemental forms must be partly removed before the elements can become matter for a new mineral, plant, or animal form. A thing does not naturally move toward something opposed to it, except when the difference is only one of greater or lesser completeness or strength. It moves only toward what completes and strengthens it.

Fire, for example, is opposed to animal life: fire burns and destroys an animal. Water, when it overwhelms an animal, drowns and kills it. The same is true of the other elements. So neither one element nor all the elements together move toward animal life. Rather, an active power frees the matter from their forms and moves it toward greater perfection. This power must be a substantial one. It cannot be, as some take Avicenna and others to mean, the quality produced by mixing the elements. An accident cannot produce a substantial change or move matter upward except by preparing it or serving as an instrument. But the question here is what actively moves it. Also, an accident depends for its existence on a substantial form. The elemental forms are therefore more fit to act and move than their qualities, which serve as their instruments. We have already shown that these forms, or any one of them, cannot be what moves matter toward animal life.

It follows that, within the elements, there is a form of the same general kind as the animal form, though not the same specific kind. It moves toward animal perfection after passing through the mineral and plant levels. Nature does not skip a level of perfection; before reaching a higher one, it passes through the lower levels. This shows that change takes place in the category of substance, and that things naturally move toward the higher spiritual realm unless something prevents them. The discussion of goals will make this clearer, God willing.
VI. Can Something Simple Both Receive and Act?

Most philosophers hold that one thing, in the same respect, cannot both receive and act. They add “in the same respect” to distinguish this from fire, which, as they put it, gives heat through its form and receives heat through its matter. We will return to this. Later philosophers say a thing can both receive and act without this qualification.

Here is the more careful view. If receiving means being affected or changed, a thing cannot be changed by itself. And if what it receives would make it more complete, it cannot make itself more complete. But if receiving means only that a thing has a feature that follows once its own nature is complete, it may bring about a feature that necessarily follows from its nature and cannot be separated from it. This is especially true of features that belong to a thing's nature, particularly a simple thing's. In such cases, the thing that produces the feature and the thing that has it are one and the same: the thing is both active and receptive in the same respect. Avicenna says this plainly in several places in his Notes. This need not apply only to simple things. A thing made of parts may also have a feature that necessarily follows from its nature; the feature does not change or make that nature more complete. In truth, features that necessarily follow from existence, like those that follow from natures, have the same source and bearer in one respect: fire and heat, water and moisture, and earth and density.

The same is true of compounds and the features that belong to them by nature. They need matter only for qualities to arise or for them to grow more complete. Fire needs matter for its nature and form, but it does not need matter to stand between being fire and being hot. Nor is there a separate cause between a thing and a feature that necessarily follows from it. If we imagine fire existing without an outside cause or a separate receiver, it would still be hot. Two arguments have been used to show that one thing cannot both receive and act. The first says that receiving and acting are two effects, so they cannot come from one thing. Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī objects that acting and being affected are not real features that need a cause, as we have already shown; and even if they were, he says, one thing could still produce two effects. I reply that both objections fail. Common sense tells us that giving and receiving are real features. Anyone who denies this is denying what is plain. The reason some call them mere ideas is that, if causing were a real feature, it would need another cause between it and its source. We answered this when discussing existence, unity, and related ideas. The second objection will be answered when we discuss whether one source can produce many things.

Another objection says that, if your rule were right, one thing could not receive one effect and produce another. You answer that this is allowed because it acts through its own nature but receives through its being affected by what it produces. Then why not say that one thing can receive and act on the same thing in different respects? If you reply that a thing cannot be affected by itself, that is the very question under debate. Why could it not act and be affected in two respects, as when a person treats himself? If you say the argument assumes one and the same respect, then it proves nothing, since the two ideas have different meanings.

I reply that philosophers have not said that a simple thing can receive one effect and produce another, so this is no counterexample to their rule. The example people imagine is an intellect standing between God and all possible things: it receives from God and acts on them. But an effect does not exist because the intellect receives existence or is acted on by it. As we explained earlier, there is no receiving or being affected in this account of existence. What is brought about is existence itself, not existence added to an essence as a feature in the world.

The mind may, however, divide a possible thing into its essence and its existence. It may then say that the essence can receive existence: first the mind considers the essence on its own, apart from existence, and then considers existence as joined to it. But when the essence is considered apart from existence in this way, how could it act on anything? This shows that when receiving is only a distinction made by the mind, the multiplicity is only in thought. When receiving occurs in reality, the receiver and what it receives are really distinct. Yet if receiving does not mean being passively affected, it may be the very same as acting.

The example of a person treating himself does not apply. This is not merely two ways of considering one thing, as when an intellect knows itself. The person has different aspects: as a doctor, with the skill and plan for treatment, he is the source of the action; as a body with the ability to be treated, he is the recipient.

The second argument says that what receives relates to what it receives as something it may receive, while an active cause relates to its effect as something that must follow. A complete cause, precisely because it is complete, makes its effect necessary. If one thing were both receiver and cause of the same effect, its relation to that effect would be both possible and necessary. These cannot both be true. If the consequences contradict each other, then the thing itself involves a contradiction.

I reply that this argument applies only to things ready to receive something, where what they receive is still only a possibility; these differ from active powers. This is what happens when things combine physically. The argument also applies in thought to natures that carry the possibility of existence, since a nature considered by itself differs from what brings it into existence. But when a thing has a feature that necessarily belongs to its nature, its relation to that feature is possible only in the broadest sense of “possible.” On the account we have given, features that necessarily belong to a thing do not overturn the argument.

Some thinkers—including al-Rāzī, the author of al-Muṭāraḥāt, and many later philosophers—allow a simple thing to be both active and receptive, and say this happens. They argue that natures give rise to features that necessarily belong to them and also bear those features. A nature must itself require a feature that necessarily belongs to it; otherwise, if the outside causes of that feature were removed, the nature could remain without it. Then the feature would not truly be necessary. The nature also bears its necessary features, since they are present in it and nowhere else. Thus possibility belongs to the natures of possible things, evenness follows from the nature of four, and a triangle's angles add up to two right angles because of the nature of a triangle.

Someone might object that these essences are composite, so one part may be the source of the feature while another part receives it. I reply, first, that every composite includes something simple, and each simple part has some feature that necessarily belongs to it—at the very least, it is a thing or is possible in the broadest sense. Second, a composite nature has its own unity. A feature that follows from the whole when its parts are together cannot be caused by just one part, or it would have appeared before the parts were joined. Nor can one part alone bear it: a triangle's surface alone cannot have angles adding up to two right angles, nor can its three sides alone. The whole triangle bears that feature, and the whole triangle brings it about. So one and the same thing is both recipient and cause in one respect.

We can also see this in descriptions everyone accepts of God: that He must exist and that He is one. His perfections—knowledge, power, and will—cannot be additions to Him. Descriptions such as “necessarily existent” and “knowing” are different: they are ideas the mind draws from His reality. So God's essence is simple, yet it is both the source of these descriptions and what they describe.

Also, according to Aristotle, the First Teacher, and his followers—including al-Fārābī and Avicenna—God’s knowledge of things consists of forms that match those things. The forms of possible things differ from God's essence, yet they are necessary consequences of it and are said to be in it. On this account, the same divine essence is both their source and their bearer.

This is where later philosophers, especially al-Rāzī, became confused. They treated “active” and “receptive” as if they meant the same thing in every use, without seeing the difference between the two cases. By treating different meanings as if they settled the matter, they set aside the proofs and fell into serious error about God's true attributes. They came to believe that these attributes are additions to the divine essence, as if the essence by itself lacked divine perfection. But the proof that God's true perfections are one with His essence and that He is one does not depend on this argument. Even if this argument did not apply to necessary features, that would not justify saying that God's perfect attributes are added to His essence. God is far above any such shortcoming.

There is another objection to the argument based on the difference between possibility and necessity. A thing's being able to receive something, the objection says, means only that it is not impossible for that thing to receive it. This is possibility in the broad sense, and it does not conflict with necessity.

The reply is that readiness means more than “not impossible.” A thing is ready to receive something only if it could receive it or fail to receive it. This is possibility in the narrower sense: the thing has not yet received what it could receive. Even if we use “possibility” in the broad sense, we cannot treat it simply as one of its two forms, necessity and this narrower kind of possibility. We use the broad meaning in a way that, in this argument, still requires the narrower kind and therefore conflicts with necessity. In short, matter that can receive a thing's existence is not the same as the active power that makes that thing necessary. No thoughtful person should deny that one and the same thing, simply as one thing, cannot receive a perfection from itself.
VII. How Thoughts Can Help Bring Things into Being

In brief, earlier discussions of powers and changing natures have shown that whatever brings bodies and their natures into existence must itself be independent of matter. Anything that exists independently of matter must be an immaterial form. So the sources of things that come into being are forms—and even thoughts.

More specifically, a soul's strong and settled thoughts can cause changes in the body without one body physically acting on another. A thought can produce heat without something hot, or cold without something cold. Several things show this. First, the power that moves a person—or an animal—is capable of producing either of two opposite actions. One cannot happen rather than the other unless something tips the choice. What tips it is the thought that one action will be pleasant or useful. That thought is what makes the action more likely. If the thought could affect the body's instruments only through another physical instrument, then its effect on that second instrument would need a third physical instrument, and so on without end. That is impossible. So a soul's thoughts can affect bodies without physical instruments standing between them.

Second, as we will see when we discuss the heavenly bodies, their movements begin with their thoughts and desires. Third, we see this in ourselves. When we decide to write, we write if nothing prevents us; the thought begins the will. When we imagine something pleasant and hope to get it, our face may redden and our body grow excited, even if the thing we hope for does not exist. When we imagine something frightening and expect it to happen, our face may pale and our body may shake, even if the thing we fear does not exist.

We also see that someone who can walk along a log laid on the ground may hesitate to cross the same log when it bridges a deep drop. They imagine falling so strongly that their power of movement obeys the thought, as it naturally obeys thoughts. Night emissions during sleep are another example.

Fourth, if a sick person becomes firmly convinced that they will recover, they may recover; if a healthy person becomes firmly convinced that they are ill, they may become ill. The gaze of a person with the evil eye is said to affect others without a physical tool. Skilled doctors are also said to treat illness through mental images and thoughts. It is told that a king once suffered a severe paralysis. His doctor knew that physical treatment would not help, so he waited for a chance to be alone with the king. Then he insulted him with harsh and vulgar words until the king became deeply upset. The king's natural heat flared up, and his body grew strong enough to fight the illness. The only cause was the king's thoughts and feelings.

Once this principle is accepted, it is easier to believe in prophecy. A soul may reach such strength and dignity that it heals the sick, makes the wicked ill, or changes one element into another—turning something that is not fire into fire. Through prayer, it may bring rain and prosperity at one time, or earthquakes and the sinking of land at another. The elements share a common matter that can receive every form. The relation of weak, individual souls to the matter of their own bodies is like the relation of powerful, more universal souls to other matter. Just as our thoughts can begin small, particular events, the thoughts of those souls may begin great events, though this is rare and strange. Talismans and magic are of the same kind. As Avicenna says, the active powers above and the receptive powers below can come together in remarkable ways.

One point related to this discussion is that a general idea cannot by itself bring about one particular action. A general idea is shared by its individual cases and relates to each of them in the same way. If it caused one rather than the others, one possible outcome would occur without a reason. That is impossible.
